symbolic names (`CSR12_MCOUNTERINTEN` -- premium's does). An empty grep
means your PATTERN missed, not that the CSR is absent: grep the NAME too
before concluding anything (a class-A trap; see the disagreement table).

Real terms from ax46mpv_advanced (line-wrapped):

```
(csr_addr == 12'h7cf) & (PERFORMANCE_MONITOR_INT == 1) & (SSCOFPMF_SUPPORT == 0)
(csr_addr == 12'h7d1) & (PERFORMANCE_MONITOR_INT == 1) & (SSCOFPMF_SUPPORT == 0) & multi_level_mode
(csr_addr == 12'h017) & (ZCE_SUPPORT_INT == 1)
(csr_addr == 12'h7c5) & (POWERBRAKE_SUPPORT_INT == 1)
```

|---|---|---|---|

| jvt 0x017 | Zcmt implemented | `ZCE_SUPPORT_INT == 1` | `NDS_ZCE_SUPPORT_INT` |

  counters). Gating 0x7CF on the perf knob alone over-claimed it on the
  Sscofpmf-bearing advanced engine and faulted the sweep.

- spec "Zcmt" is the `ZCE_SUPPORT` knob, NOT the CoDense knob.

2. vsim knob binding: `src/hybrid/andes_caps_config.hpp`

4. the caps unit test modeling THIS engine's config shape

(engine-registration.md has the full contract):

| Class | Signature | Action |
|---|---|---|
| A. Never silently absorb it |
| D. Suspected spec error / ambiguity | independent implementations (RTL AND QEMU) agree against the spec text, or the spec self-contradicts | record the chosen reading + escalate to the spec owners |

way (section vs Table 13; grep vs the probe); (2) QEMU as an independent
implementation of the same spec; (3) sibling engines (does premium's RTL
carry the same term?); (4) the empirical sweep/probe -- execution evidence
outranks any reading.

Evidence standard for the report: verbatim quotes with file:line / PDF
page for every claim in a discrepancy row. A paraphrase cannot be
re-audited, and class A errors hide in paraphrases.

## Worked example: the 0x7CF find, end to end

1	# Engine registration: per-engine, per-config test completeness
2	
3	The authoritative contract lives IN THE REPO at `tests/engines/README.md`
4	(registration inputs/artifacts/checks, the report format including the
5	mandatory Discrepancies section, and the deregistration checklist for
6	removing an engine + its report + its test cases). This reference explains
7	the mechanics behind it. If the two ever disagree, the repo contract wins
8	-- update this file.
9	
10	andesim ships commercially. "The transport machinery is tested" is not the
11	same as "THIS engine build's CSR set is tested" -- every engine can differ
12	in its CSR set, and the same core built with a different config differs
13	again. Registration turns "nothing missed" from a convention into a set of
14	checks that fail.
15	
16	## Identity: an engine build = (core, config)
17	
18	The registration key is the engine name plus a short hash of the BUILD
19	`config.inc` (`build/V<engine>/obj_sc/config.inc` -- the file Phase 0
20	already reads). Layout in the andesim repo:
21	
22	```
23	tests/engines/<engine>-<confighash8>/
24	├── engine.env               # engine name, QEMU -cpu pairing, march, vlen, priv levels
25	├── rtl_params.json          # resolved RTL params: data for the shared generator's
26	│                            #   EXCL_SIDEFX-only RTL fallback (provenance in "notes")
27	├── csr_manifest.csv         # deliverable 1 (tests/engines/gen_manifest.py <regdir>;
28	│                            #   the shared generator auto-runs the probe)
29	├── csr_restore_table.md     # human-readable restore view of the manifest
30	│                            #   (generated by render_restore_table.py; drift-guarded)
31	├── registration_report.md   # the CSR report (see the repo contract)
32	└── fixtures/                # deliverable 3 (generated)
33	```
34	
35	A rebuilt config produces a different hash -> a different directory -> the
36	guard (deliverable 4) refuses to run the engine against the old artifacts.
37	Nothing about "same core, new config" can be silently reused.
38	
39	## Deliverable 1: the CSR manifest
40	
41	One row per spec-inventory CSR (all of them, not just transported ones):
42	
43	```
44	addr,name,access,exists_cond,implemented,transported,gate_or_disposition,reset_value
45	0x7D1,mcountermask_m,MRW,PMNDS&misa[20],no,no,UMODE(off),-
46	0x7CF,mcounterinten,MRW,PMNDS,yes,yes,PERF_MONITOR,0x0
47	...
48	```
49	
50	The manifest is produced by ONE shared generator --
51	`python3 tests/engines/gen_manifest.py <regdir>` -- which reads the regdir's
52	`engine.env` (identity) and `rtl_params.json` (resolved RTL params for the
53	SIDEFX-only fallback below). There is no per-engine generator code.
54	
55	Column sources -- each answers a different question and they must agree:
56	- `exists_cond`: the SPA (per-CSR IM Requirement / Table 13) -- Phase 1.
57	- `implemented`: MEASURED -- the generator auto-runs the probe (below);
58	  never inferred from QEMU, never modeled from config knobs. The RTL
59	  `existent_csr` equation is consulted ONLY for the EXCL_SIDEFX CSRs the
60	  probe must skip; any other CSR missing from the probe fails the run
61	  (`test_gen_manifest_probe.sh` pins both behaviors).
62	- `transported`: the caps verdict (`--describe andes_csrs` of THIS binary).
63	- `reset_value`: MEASURED -- the probe's reset-hart read. This IS the
64	  engine's reset value table: generated, reviewed by a human once against
65	  the spec's reset column (IM/DC fields will differ from the spec -- that
66	  is expected and fine), then committed.
67	
68	## Deliverable 2: the both-direction completeness check
69	
70	- **Over-claim** (caps says yes, RTL says no): already caught empirically --
71	  the cold-cache capture's CSR sweep faults and names the CSR. Keep a
72	  cold-cache hybrid run in the engine's registered test set so this is a
73	  TEST, not an incident.
74	- **Under-claim** (RTL has it, caps gates it off -- the silent state-loss
75	  case): script it from the manifest. Every row with
76	  `exists_cond == true against this config.inc` (or `implemented == yes`
77	  from the probe) must have `transported == yes` OR a named `EXCL_*`
78	  disposition from the coverage matrix. A row with neither FAILS. This is
79	  the "nothing missed" enforcement -- no human list-checking.
80	
81	**The probe.** A checked read of every inventory CSR on the halted,
82	freshly reset hart (the DM mirrors an unimplemented CSR as a cmderr, which
83	`read_register_64_checked` reports as nullopt) yields the implemented set
84	plus reset values in one pass (~232 reads, seconds of sim time). It is
85	`tests/engines/probe_engine.sh <engine>` -> `sim_<engine> --probe`, and the
86	manifest generator runs it automatically (set ANDESIM_PROBE_CSV only to
87	reuse a capture). EXCL_SIDEFX rows (reads with side effects) are skipped by
88	policy and are the ONLY rows allowed to fall back to the RTL equation.
89	Reset-time accessibility is handled inside the probe: it enables
90	mstatus.FS/VS before reading, else FP/V CSRs would mis-probe as absent.
91	
92	## Deliverable 3: generated per-engine fixtures
93	
94	Write-survival tests must exist per engine and must come from a GENERATOR
95	keyed by the manifest, not from hand-written files -- hand-written sets rot
96	and miss CSRs. For each transported read/write CSR: write a distinctive
97	value before the ROI (proves resume restores it) and inside the ROI (proves
98	drain captures it), assert via the drained state and `--verify`.
99	
100	The generator needs a per-CSR safe-write policy, because blind writes to
101	control CSRs break the run (mcache_ctl flips caches, milmb/mdlmb move local
102	memory, mhsp_ctl arms stack protection). Policy tiers:
103	- plain state (scratch-like, masks, event selects): write a full
104	  distinctive pattern;
105	- WARL-constrained: write within a reviewed mask;
106	- dangerous control CSRs: skip-list with a comment saying why -- the
107	  round-trip of these is still covered by --verify on real workload values.
108	The policy table is reviewed once and committed next to the generator.
109	
110	## Deliverable 4: the registration guard
111	
112	A script that cross-checks: every engine `./andesim list engines` reports
113	must have a `tests/engines/<engine>-<confighash8>/` whose hash matches the
114	CURRENT binary's config.inc, with a manifest and generated fixtures
115	present. Unregistered or stale-hash engines fail with "run the bring-up
116	registration". Wire it next to the existing coverage guard so CI runs both.
117	
118	## Matrix runner
119	
120	The full 47-fixture suite stays on the default engines (wall-time). Every
121	REGISTERED engine runs its own core set on every suite run: the probe
122	check, its generated CSR fixtures, a cold-cache hybrid run (the sweep
123	validator), and one --verify run. `run_e2e.sh` takes the engine axis from
124	the registration dirs, so adding a registration automatically adds its
125	tests -- no runner edit, nothing to forget.
126

├── rtl_params.json          # resolved RTL params: data for the shared generator's
│                            #   EXCL_SIDEFX-only RTL fallback (provenance in "notes")
├── csr_manifest.csv         # deliverable 1 (tests/engines/gen_manifest.py <regdir>;
│                            #   the shared generator auto-runs the probe)
├── csr_restore_table.md     # human-readable restore view of the manifest
│                            #   (generated by render_restore_table.py; drift-guarded)
├── registration_report.md   # the CSR report (see the repo contract)
└── fixtures/                # deliverable 3 (generated)
```

A rebuilt config produces a different hash -> a different directory -> the
guard (deliverable 4) refuses to run the engine against the old artifacts.
Nothing about "same core, new config" can be silently reused.

## Deliverable 1: the CSR manifest

One row per spec-inventory CSR (all of them, not just transported ones):

```
addr,name,access,exists_cond,implemented,transported,gate_or_disposition,reset_value
0x7D1,mcountermask_m,MRW,PMNDS&misa[20],no,no,UMODE(off),-
0x7CF,mcounterinten,MRW,PMNDS,yes,yes,PERF_MONITOR,0x0
...
```

The manifest is produced by ONE shared generator --
`python3 tests/engines/gen_manifest.py <regdir>` -- which reads the regdir's
`engine.env` (identity) and `rtl_params.json` (resolved RTL params for the
SIDEFX-only fallback below). There is no per-engine generator code.

Column sources -- each answers a different question and they must agree:
- `exists_cond`: the SPA (per-CSR IM Requirement / Table 13) -- Phase 1.
- `implemented`: MEASURED -- the generator auto-runs the probe (below);
  never inferred from QEMU, never modeled from config knobs. The RTL
  `existent_csr` equation is consulted ONLY for the EXCL_SIDEFX CSRs the
  probe must skip; any other CSR missing from the probe fails the run
  (`test_gen_manifest_probe.sh` pins both behaviors).
- `transported`: the caps verdict (`--describe andes_csrs` of THIS binary).
- `reset_value`: MEASURED -- the probe's reset-hart read. This IS the
  engine's reset value table: generated, reviewed by a human once against
  the spec's reset column (IM/DC fields will differ from the spec -- that
  is expected and fine), then committed.

## Deliverable 2: the both-direction completeness check

- **Over-claim** (caps says yes, RTL says no): already caught empirically --
  the cold-cache capture's CSR sweep faults and names the CSR. Keep a
  cold-cache hybrid run in the engine's registered test set so this is a
  TEST, not an incident.
- **Under-claim** (RTL has it, caps gates it off -- the silent state-loss
  case): script it from the manifest. Every row with
  `exists_cond == true against this config.inc` (or `implemented == yes`
  from the probe) must have `transported == yes` OR a named `EXCL_*`
  disposition from the coverage matrix. A row with neither FAILS. This is
  the "nothing missed" enforcement -- no human list-checking.

**The probe.** A checked read of every inventory CSR on the halted,
freshly reset hart (the DM mirrors an unimplemented CSR as a cmderr, which
`read_register_64_checked` reports as nullopt) yields the implemented set
plus reset values in one pass (~232 reads, seconds of sim time). It is
`tests/engines/probe_engine.sh <engine>` -> `sim_<engine> --probe`, and the
manifest generator runs it automatically (set ANDESIM_PROBE_CSV only to
reuse a capture). EXCL_SIDEFX rows (reads with side effects) are skipped by
policy and are the ONLY rows allowed to fall back to the RTL equation.
Reset-time accessibility is handled inside the probe: it enables
mstatus.FS/VS before reading, else FP/V CSRs would mis-probe as absent.

## Deliverable 3: generated per-engine fixtures

Write-survival tests must exist per engine and must come from a GENERATOR
keyed by the manifest, not from hand-written files -- hand-written sets rot
and miss CSRs. For each transported read/write CSR: write a distinctive
value before the ROI (proves resume restores it) and inside the ROI (proves
drain captures it), assert via the drained state and `--verify`.

The generator needs a per-CSR safe-write policy, because blind writes to
control CSRs break the run (mcache_ctl flips caches, milmb/mdlmb move local
memory, mhsp_ctl arms stack protection). Policy tiers:
- plain state (scratch-like, masks, event selects): write a full
  distinctive pattern;
- WARL-constrained: write within a reviewed mask;
- dangerous control CSRs: skip-list with a comment saying why -- the
  round-trip of these is still covered by --verify on real workload values.
The policy table is reviewed once and committed next to the generator.

## Deliverable 4: the registration guard

A script that cross-checks: every engine `./andesim list engines` reports
must have a `tests/engines/<engine>-<confighash8>/` whose hash matches the
CURRENT binary's config.inc, with a manifest and generated fixtures
present. Unregistered or stale-hash engines fail with "run the bring-up
registration". Wire it next to the existing coverage guard so CI runs both.

## Matrix runner

The full 47-fixture suite stays on the default engines (wall-time). Every
REGISTERED engine runs its own core set on every suite run: the probe
check, its generated CSR fixtures, a cold-cache hybrid run (the sweep
validator), and one --verify run. `run_e2e.sh` takes the engine axis from
the registration dirs, so adding a registration automatically adds its
tests -- no runner edit, nothing to forget.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/nick/.claude/skills/skill-creator

# Skill Creator

A skill for creating new skills and iteratively improving them.

At a high level, the process of creating a skill goes like this:

- Decide what you want the skill to do and roughly how it should do it
- Write a draft of the skill
- Create a few test prompts and run claude-with-access-to-the-skill on them
- Help the user evaluate the results both qualitatively and quantitatively
  - While the runs happen in the background, draft some quantitative evals if there aren't any (if there are some, you can either use as is or modify if you feel something needs to change about them). Then explain them to the user (or if they already existed, explain the ones that already exist)
  - Use the `eval-viewer/generate_review.py` script to show the user the results for them to look at, and also let them look at the quantitative metrics
- Rewrite the skill based on feedback from the user's evaluation of the results (and also if there are any glaring flaws that become apparent from the quantitative benchmarks)
- Repeat until you're satisfied
- Expand the test set and try again at larger scale

Your job when using this skill is to figure out where the user is in this process and then jump in and help them progress through these stages. So for instance, maybe they're like "I want to make a skill for X". You can help narrow down what they mean, write a draft, write the test cases, figure out how they want to evaluate, run all the prompts, and repeat.

On the other hand, maybe they already have a draft of the skill. In this case you can go straight to the eval/iterate part of the loop.

Of course, you should always be flexible and if the user is like "I don't need to run a bunch of evaluations, just vibe with me", you can do that instead.

Then after the skill is done (but again, the order is flexible), you can also run the skill description improver, which we have a whole separate script for, to optimize the triggering of the skill.

Cool? Cool.

## Communicating with the user

The skill creator is liable to be used by people across a wide range of familiarity with coding jargon. If you haven't heard (and how could you, it's only very recently that it started), there's a trend now where the power of Claude is inspiring plumbers to open up their terminals, parents and grandparents to google "how to install npm". On the other hand, the bulk of users are probably fairly computer-literate.

So please pay attention to context cues to understand how to phrase your communication! In the default case, just to give you some idea:

- "evaluation" and "benchmark" are borderline, but OK
- for "JSON" and "assertion" you want to see serious cues from the user that they know what those things are before using them without explaining them

It's OK to briefly explain terms if you're in doubt, and feel free to clarify terms with a short definition if you're unsure if the user will get it.

---

## Creating a skill

### Capture Intent

Start by understanding the user's intent. The current conversation might already contain a workflow the user wants to capture (e.g., they say "turn this into a skill"). If so, extract answers from the conversation history first — the tools used, the sequence of steps, corrections the user made, input/output formats observed. The user may need to fill the gaps, and should confirm before proceeding to the next step.

1. What should this skill enable Claude to do?
2. When should this skill trigger? (what user phrases/contexts)
3. What's the expected output format?
4. Should we set up test cases to verify the skill works? Skills with objectively verifiable outputs (file transforms, data extraction, code generation, fixed workflow steps) benefit from test cases. Skills with subjective outputs (writing style, art) often don't need them. Suggest the appropriate default based on the skill type, but let the user decide.

### Interview and Research

Proactively ask questions about edge cases, input/output formats, example files, success criteria, and dependencies. Wait to write test prompts until you've got this part ironed out.

Check available MCPs - if useful for research (searching docs, finding similar skills, looking up best practices), research in parallel via subagents if available, otherwise inline. Come prepared with context to reduce burden on the user.

### Write the SKILL.md

Based on the user interview, fill in these components:

- **name**: Skill identifier
- **description**: When to trigger, what it does. This is the primary triggering mechanism - include both what the skill does AND specific contexts for when to use it. All "when to use" info goes here, not in the body. Note: currently Claude has a tendency to "undertrigger" skills -- to not use them when they'd be useful. To combat this, please make the skill descriptions a little bit "pushy". So for instance, instead of "How to build a simple fast dashboard to display internal Anthropic data.", you might write "How to build a simple fast dashboard to display internal Anthropic data. Make sure to use this skill whenever the user mentions dashboards, data visualization, internal metrics, or wants to display any kind of company data, even if they don't explicitly ask for a 'dashboard.'"
- **compatibility**: Required tools, dependencies (optional, rarely needed)
- **the rest of the skill :)**

### Skill Writing Guide

#### Anatomy of a Skill

```
skill-name/
├── SKILL.md (required)
│   ├── YAML frontmatter (name, description required)
│   └── Markdown instructions
└── Bundled Resources (optional)
    ├── scripts/    - Executable code for deterministic/repetitive tasks
    ├── references/ - Docs loaded into context as needed
    └── assets/     - Files used in output (templates, icons, fonts)
```

#### Progressive Disclosure

Skills use a three-level loading system:
1. **Metadata** (name + description) - Always in context (~100 words)
2. **SKILL.md body** - In context whenever skill triggers (<500 lines ideal)
3. **Bundled resources** - As needed (unlimited, scripts can execute without loading)

These word counts are approximate and you can feel free to go longer if needed.

**Key patterns:**
- Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines; if you're approaching this limit, add an additional layer of hierarchy along with clear pointers about where the model using the skill should go next to follow up.
- Reference files clearly from SKILL.md with guidance on when to read them
- For large reference files (>300 lines), include a table of contents

**Domain organization**: When a skill supports multiple domains/frameworks, organize by variant:
```
cloud-deploy/
├── SKILL.md (workflow + selection)
└── references/
    ├── aws.md
    ├── gcp.md
    └── azure.md
```
Claude reads only the relevant reference file.

#### Principle of Lack of Surprise

This goes without saying, but skills must not contain malware, exploit code, or any content that could compromise system security. A skill's contents should not surprise the user in their intent if described. Don't go along with requests to create misleading skills or skills designed to facilitate unauthorized access, data exfiltration, or other malicious activities. Things like a "roleplay as an XYZ" are OK though.

#### Writing Patterns

Prefer using the imperative form in instructions.

**Defining output formats** - You can do it like this:
```markdown
## Report structure
ALWAYS use this exact template:
# [Title]
## Executive summary
## Key findings
## Recommendations
```

**Examples pattern** - It's useful to include examples. You can format them like this (but if "Input" and "Output" are in the examples you might want to deviate a little):
```markdown
## Commit message format
**Example 1:**
Input: Added user authentication with JWT tokens
Output: feat(auth): implement JWT-based authentication
```

### Writing Style

Try to explain to the model why things are important in lieu of heavy-handed musty MUSTs. Use theory of mind and try to make the skill general and not super-narrow to specific examples. Start by writing a draft and then look at it with fresh eyes and improve it.

### Test Cases

After writing the skill draft, come up with 2-3 realistic test prompts — the kind of thing a real user would actually say. Share them with the user: [you don't have to use this exact language] "Here are a few test cases I'd like to try. Do these look right, or do you want to add more?" Then run them.

Save test cases to `evals/evals.json`. Don't write assertions yet — just the prompts. You'll draft assertions in the next step while the runs are in progress.

```json
{
  "skill_name": "example-skill",
  "evals": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "prompt": "User's task prompt",
      "expected_output": "Description of expected result",
      "files": []
    }
  ]
}
```

See `references/schemas.md` for the full schema (including the `assertions` field, which you'll add later).

## Running and evaluating test cases

This section is one continuous sequence — don't stop partway through. Do NOT use `/skill-test` or any other testing skill.

Put results in `<skill-name>-workspace/` as a sibling to the skill directory. Within the workspace, organize results by iteration (`iteration-1/`, `iteration-2/`, etc.) and within that, each test case gets a directory (`eval-0/`, `eval-1/`, etc.). Don't create all of this upfront — just create directories as you go.

### Step 1: Spawn all runs (with-skill AND baseline) in the same turn

For each test case, spawn two subagents in the same turn — one with the skill, one without. This is important: don't spawn the with-skill runs first and then come back for baselines later. Launch everything at once so it all finishes around the same time.

**With-skill run:**

```
Execute this task:
- Skill path: <path-to-skill>
- Task: <eval prompt>
- Input files: <eval files if any, or "none">
- Save outputs to: <workspace>/iteration-<N>/eval-<ID>/with_skill/outputs/
- Outputs to save: <what the user cares about — e.g., "the .docx file", "the final CSV">
```

**Baseline run** (same prompt, but the baseline depends on context):
- **Creating a new skill**: no skill at all. Same prompt, no skill path, save to `without_skill/outputs/`.
- **Improving an existing skill**: the old version. Before editing, snapshot the skill (`cp -r <skill-path> <workspace>/skill-snapshot/`), then point the baseline subagent at the snapshot. Save to `old_skill/outputs/`.

Write an `eval_metadata.json` for each test case (assertions can be empty for now). Give each eval a descriptive name based on what it's testing — not just "eval-0". Use this name for the directory too. If this iteration uses new or modified eval prompts, create these files for each new eval directory — don't assume they carry over from previous iterations.

```json
{
  "eval_id": 0,
  "eval_name": "descriptive-name-here",
  "prompt": "The user's task prompt",
  "assertions": []
}
```

### Step 2: While runs are in progress, draft assertions

Don't just wait for the runs to finish — you can use this time productively. Draft quantitative assertions for each test case and explain them to the user. If assertions already exist in `evals/evals.json`, review them and explain what they check.

Good assertions are objectively verifiable and have descriptive names — they should read clearly in the benchmark viewer so someone glancing at the results immediately understands what each one checks. Subjective skills (writing style, design quality) are better evaluated qualitatively — don't force assertions onto things that need human judgment.

Update the `eval_metadata.json` files and `evals/evals.json` with the assertions once drafted. Also explain to the user what they'll see in the viewer — both the qualitative outputs and the quantitative benchmark.

### Step 3: As runs complete, capture timing data

When each subagent task completes, you receive a notification containing `total_tokens` and `duration_ms`. Save this data immediately to `timing.json` in the run directory:

```json
{
  "total_tokens": 84852,
  "duration_ms": 23332,
  "total_duration_seconds": 23.3
}
```

This is the only opportunity to capture this data — it comes through the task notification and isn't persisted elsewhere. Process each notification as it arrives rather than trying to batch them.

### Step 4: Grade, aggregate, and launch the viewer

Once all runs are done:

1. **Grade each run** — spawn a grader subagent (or grade inline) that reads `agents/grader.md` and evaluates each assertion against the outputs. Save results to `grading.json` in each run directory. The grading.json expectations array must use the fields `text`, `passed`, and `evidence` (not `name`/`met`/`details` or other variants) — the viewer depends on these exact field names. For assertions that can be checked programmatically, write and run a script rather than eyeballing it — scripts are faster, more reliable, and can be reused across iterations.

2. **Aggregate into benchmark** — run the aggregation script from the skill-creator directory:
   ```bash
   python -m scripts.aggregate_benchmark <workspace>/iteration-N --skill-name <name>
   ```
   This produces `benchmark.json` and `benchmark.md` with pass_rate, time, and tokens for each configuration, with mean ± stddev and the delta. If generating benchmark.json manually, see `references/schemas.md` for the exact schema the viewer expects.
Put each with_skill version before its baseline counterpart.

3. **Do an analyst pass** — read the benchmark data and surface patterns the aggregate stats might hide. See `agents/analyzer.md` (the "Analyzing Benchmark Results" section) for what to look for — things like assertions that always pass regardless of skill (non-discriminating), high-variance evals (possibly flaky), and time/token tradeoffs.

4. **Launch the viewer** with both qualitative outputs and quantitative data:
   ```bash
   nohup python <skill-creator-path>/eval-viewer/generate_review.py \
     <workspace>/iteration-N \
     --skill-name "my-skill" \
     --benchmark <workspace>/iteration-N/benchmark.json \
     > /dev/null 2>&1 &
   VIEWER_PID=$!
   ```
   For iteration 2+, also pass `--previous-workspace <workspace>/iteration-<N-1>`.

   **Cowork / headless environments:** If `webbrowser.open()` is not available or the environment has no display, use `--static <output_path>` to write a standalone HTML file instead of starting a server. Feedback will be downloaded as a `feedback.json` file when the user clicks "Submit All Reviews". After download, copy `feedback.json` into the workspace directory for the next iteration to pick up.

Note: please use generate_review.py to create the viewer; there's no need to write custom HTML.

5. **Tell the user** something like: "I've opened the results in your browser. There are two tabs — 'Outputs' lets you click through each test case and leave feedback, 'Benchmark' shows the quantitative comparison. When you're done, come back here and let me know."

### What the user sees in the viewer

The "Outputs" tab shows one test case at a time:
- **Prompt**: the task that was given
- **Output**: the files the skill produced, rendered inline where possible
- **Previous Output** (iteration 2+): collapsed section showing last iteration's output
- **Formal Grades** (if grading was run): collapsed section showing assertion pass/fail
- **Feedback**: a textbox that auto-saves as they type
- **Previous Feedback** (iteration 2+): their comments from last time, shown below the textbox

The "Benchmark" tab shows the stats summary: pass rates, timing, and token usage for each configuration, with per-eval breakdowns and analyst observations.

Navigation is via prev/next buttons or arrow keys. When done, they click "Submit All Reviews" which saves all feedback to `feedback.json`.

### Step 5: Read the feedback

When the user tells you they're done, read `feedback.json`:

```json
{
  "reviews": [
    {"run_id": "eval-0-with_skill", "feedback": "the chart is missing axis labels", "timestamp": "..."},
    {"run_id": "eval-1-with_skill", "feedback": "", "timestamp": "..."},
    {"run_id": "eval-2-with_skill", "feedback": "perfect, love this", "timestamp": "..."}
  ],
  "status": "complete"
}
```

Empty feedback means the user thought it was fine. Focus your improvements on the test cases where the user had specific complaints.

Kill the viewer server when you're done with it:

```bash
kill $VIEWER_PID 2>/dev/null
```

---

## Improving the skill

This is the heart of the loop. You've run the test cases, the user has reviewed the results, and now you need to make the skill better based on their feedback.

### How to think about improvements

1. **Generalize from the feedback.** The big picture thing that's happening here is that we're trying to create skills that can be used a million times (maybe literally, maybe even more who knows) across many different prompts. Here you and the user are iterating on only a few examples over and over again because it helps move faster. The user knows these examples in and out and it's quick for them to assess new outputs. But if the skill you and the user are codeveloping works only for those examples, it's useless. Rather than put in fiddly overfitty changes, or oppressively constrictive MUSTs, if there's some stubborn issue, you might try branching out and using different metaphors, or recommending different patterns of working. It's relatively cheap to try and maybe you'll land on something great.

2. **Keep the prompt lean.** Remove things that aren't pulling their weight. Make sure to read the transcripts, not just the final outputs — if it looks like the skill is making the model waste a bunch of time doing things that are unproductive, you can try getting rid of the parts of the skill that are making it do that and seeing what happens.

3. **Explain the why.** Try hard to explain the **why** behind everything you're asking the model to do. Today's LLMs are *smart*. They have good theory of mind and when given a good harness can go beyond rote instructions and really make things happen. Even if the feedback from the user is terse or frustrated, try to actually understand the task and why the user is writing what they wrote, and what they actually wrote, and then transmit this understanding into the instructions. If you find yourself writing ALWAYS or NEVER in all caps, or using super rigid structures, that's a yellow flag — if possible, reframe and explain the reasoning so that the model understands why the thing you're asking for is important. That's a more humane, powerful, and effective approach.

4. **Look for repeated work across test cases.** Read the transcripts from the test runs and notice if the subagents all independently wrote similar helper scripts or took the same multi-step approach to something. If all 3 test cases resulted in the subagent writing a `create_docx.py` or a `build_chart.py`, that's a strong signal the skill should bundle that script. Write it once, put it in `scripts/`, and tell the skill to use it. This saves every future invocation from reinventing the wheel.

This task is pretty important (we are trying to create billions a year in economic value here!) and your thinking time is not the blocker; take your time and really mull things over. I'd suggest writing a draft revision and then looking at it anew and making improvements. Really do your best to get into the head of the user and understand what they want and need.

### The iteration loop

After improving the skill:

1. Apply your improvements to the skill
2. Rerun all test cases into a new `iteration-<N+1>/` directory, including baseline runs. If you're creating a new skill, the baseline is always `without_skill` (no skill) — that stays the same across iterations. If you're improving an existing skill, use your judgment on what makes sense as the baseline: the original version the user came in with, or the previous iteration.
3. Launch the reviewer with `--previous-workspace` pointing at the previous iteration
4. Wait for the user to review and tell you they're done
5. Read the new feedback, improve again, repeat

Keep going until:
- The user says they're happy
- The feedback is all empty (everything looks good)
- You're not making meaningful progress

---

## Advanced: Blind comparison

For situations where you want a more rigorous comparison between two versions of a skill (e.g., the user asks "is the new version actually better?"), there's a blind comparison system. Read `agents/comparator.md` and `agents/analyzer.md` for the details. The basic idea is: give two outputs to an independent agent without telling it which is which, and let it judge quality. Then analyze why the winner won.

This is optional, requires subagents, and most users won't need it. The human review loop is usually sufficient.

---

## Description Optimization

The description field in SKILL.md frontmatter is the primary mechanism that determines whether Claude invokes a skill. After creating or improving a skill, offer to optimize the description for better triggering accuracy.

### Step 1: Generate trigger eval queries

Create 20 eval queries — a mix of should-trigger and should-not-trigger. Save as JSON:

```json
[
  {"query": "the user prompt", "should_trigger": true},
  {"query": "another prompt", "should_trigger": false}
]
```

The queries must be realistic and something a Claude Code or Claude.ai user would actually type. Not abstract requests, but requests that are concrete and specific and have a good amount of detail. For instance, file paths, personal context about the user's job or situation, column names and values, company names, URLs. A little bit of backstory. Some might be in lowercase or contain abbreviations or typos or casual speech. Use a mix of different lengths, and focus on edge cases rather than making them clear-cut (the user will get a chance to sign off on them).

Bad: `"Format this data"`, `"Extract text from PDF"`, `"Create a chart"`

Good: `"ok so my boss just sent me this xlsx file (its in my downloads, called something like 'Q4 sales final FINAL v2.xlsx') and she wants me to add a column that shows the profit margin as a percentage. The revenue is in column C and costs are in column D i think"`

For the **should-trigger** queries (8-10), think about coverage. You want different phrasings of the same intent — some formal, some casual. Include cases where the user doesn't explicitly name the skill or file type but clearly needs it. Throw in some uncommon use cases and cases where this skill competes with another but should win.

For the **should-not-trigger** queries (8-10), the most valuable ones are the near-misses — queries that share keywords or concepts with the skill but actually need something different. Think adjacent domains, ambiguous phrasing where a naive keyword match would trigger but shouldn't, and cases where the query touches on something the skill does but in a context where another tool is more appropriate.

The key thing to avoid: don't make should-not-trigger queries obviously irrelevant. "Write a fibonacci function" as a negative test for a PDF skill is too easy — it doesn't test anything. The negative cases should be genuinely tricky.

### Step 2: Review with user

Present the eval set to the user for review using the HTML template:

1. Read the template from `assets/eval_review.html`
2. Replace the placeholders:
   - `__EVAL_DATA_PLACEHOLDER__` → the JSON array of eval items (no quotes around it — it's a JS variable assignment)
   - `__SKILL_NAME_PLACEHOLDER__` → the skill's name
   - `__SKILL_DESCRIPTION_PLACEHOLDER__` → the skill's current description
3. Write to a temp file (e.g., `/tmp/eval_review_<skill-name>.html`) and open it: `open /tmp/eval_review_<skill-name>.html`
4. The user can edit queries, toggle should-trigger, add/remove entries, then click "Export Eval Set"
5. The file downloads to `~/Downloads/eval_set.json` — check the Downloads folder for the most recent version in case there are multiple (e.g., `eval_set (1).json`)

This step matters — bad eval queries lead to bad descriptions.

### Step 3: Run the optimization loop

Tell the user: "This will take some time — I'll run the optimization loop in the background and check on it periodically."

Save the eval set to the workspace, then run in the background:

```bash
python -m scripts.run_loop \
  --eval-set <path-to-trigger-eval.json> \
  --skill-path <path-to-skill> \
  --model <model-id-powering-this-session> \
  --max-iterations 5 \
  --verbose
```

Use the model ID from your system prompt (the one powering the current session) so the triggering test matches what the user actually experiences.

While it runs, periodically tail the output to give the user updates on which iteration it's on and what the scores look like.

This handles the full optimization loop automatically. It re-evaluates each new description on both train and test, iterating up to 5 times. When it's done, it opens an HTML report in the browser showing the results per iteration and returns JSON with `best_description` — selected by test score rather than train score to avoid overfitting.

Understanding the triggering mechanism helps design better eval queries. Skills appear in Claude's `available_skills` list with their name + description, and Claude decides whether to consult a skill based on that description. The important thing to know is that Claude only consults skills for tasks it can't easily handle on its own — simple, one-step queries like "read this PDF" may not trigger a skill even if the description matches perfectly, because Claude can handle them directly with basic tools. Complex, multi-step, or specialized queries reliably trigger skills when the description matches.

This means your eval queries should be substantive enough that Claude would actually benefit from consulting a skill. Simple queries like "read file X" are poor test cases — they won't trigger skills regardless of description quality.

# CSR transport bring-up for a new Andes core

Inputs you need from the user (ask if missing):
- The AndeStar V5 SPA PDF for the core family (the repo carries
  `AndeStar_V5_SPA_UM164_V1.7.pdf` for the current cores).
- The engine name (e.g. `ax45mpv_premium`) and a built vsim checkout
  (`VSIM_BIN_DIR` in `config.env` points at its `build/`).
- Optionally the matching QEMU `-cpu` name for the oracle leg.

The goal: every CSR the core implements and the ROI can touch is restored at
resume, re-read at drain, and `--verify`-compared -- and every CSR the core
does NOT implement is gated off, because the batched Program-Buffer sweep
faults (cmderr=3) on a single over-claimed CSR.

Work in this order. Each phase has a reference file with the details --
read it when you reach the phase, not before.

## Phase 0: establish ground truth (three sources)

Validation means connecting THREE sources per CSR -- the spec, the build
config, and the CPU core RTL -- and they speak different languages:
- CONFIG: `$VSIM_BIN_DIR/V<engine>/obj_sc/config.inc` (the BUILD copy -- the
  `external/` source tree can differ) + `sim_<engine> --describe`.
- RTL: the CSR decoder's `existent_csr` equation (kv_core family:
  `andes_ip/kv_core/ucore/hdl/kv_csr_dec.v`). This is the Rosetta stone: it
  states each spec existence condition as a function of config params --
  the mapping neither document contains.
- SPEC: Phase 1 below.
Read `references/three-way-audit.md` -- the tutorial for connecting the
three and turning the result into the engine's test cases. Do not trust
QEMU: its gdbstub exposes CSRs the vsim RTL does not implement, and
restoring or sweeping one of those stalls or faults the Debug Module.

## Phase 1: mine the spec

Run `scripts/extract_csr_inventory.py <spec.pdf>` to refresh
`tests/andes_csr/csr_inventory.csv` (needs PyMuPDF; use a venv). Then pull,
for each CSR the core claims: the IM Requirement (existence condition), the
Access Mode, and the reset value. The SPA has a fixed per-CSR layout and a
consolidated existence table (Table 13) -- see
`references/spec-mining.md` for the exact headers and extraction recipes.

  field mismatches on Andes/M-ext CSRs -- even if they do not say "bring-up"

# CSR transport bring-up for a new Andes core

Inputs you need from the user (ask if missing):
- The AndeStar V5 SPA PDF for the core family (the repo carries
  `AndeStar_V5_SPA_UM164_V1.7.pdf` for the current cores).
- The engine name (e.g. `ax45mpv_premium`) and a built vsim checkout
  (`VSIM_BIN_DIR` in `config.env` points at its `build/`).
- Optionally the matching QEMU `-cpu` name for the oracle leg.

The goal: every CSR the core implements and the ROI can touch is restored at
resume, re-read at drain, and `--verify`-compared -- and every CSR the core
does NOT implement is gated off. Getting the gate wrong is SILENT at run
time: transport is one tolerant Abstract Command per CSR in both directions
(the Program Buffer carries only the V data sweep, the Tier-B vsetvl, and
L2C MMIO), so an over-claimed CSR just mirrors as zero. Caps truth is proven
by the reset-hart probe + the manifest completeness check, never by a run
"not crashing".

Work in this order. Each phase has a reference file with the details --
read it when you reach the phase, not before.

## Phase 0: establish ground truth (three sources)

Validation means connecting THREE sources per CSR -- the spec, the build
config, and the CPU core RTL -- and they speak different languages:
- CONFIG: `$VSIM_BIN_DIR/V<engine>/obj_sc/config.inc` (the BUILD copy -- the
  `external/` source tree can differ) + `sim_<engine> --describe`.
- RTL: the CSR decoder's `existent_csr` equation (kv_core family:
  `andes_ip/kv_core/ucore/hdl/kv_csr_dec.v`). This is the Rosetta stone: it
  states each spec existence condition as a function of config params --
  the mapping neither document contains.
- SPEC: Phase 1 below.
Read `references/three-way-audit.md` -- the tutorial for connecting the
three and turning the result into the engine's test cases. Do not trust
QEMU: its gdbstub exposes CSRs the vsim RTL does not implement, and
restoring or sweeping one of those stalls or faults the Debug Module.

## Phase 1: mine the spec

Run `scripts/extract_csr_inventory.py <spec.pdf>` to refresh
`tests/andes_csr/csr_inventory.csv` (needs PyMuPDF; use a venv). Then pull,
for each CSR the core claims: the IM Requirement (existence condition), the
Access Mode, and the reset value. The SPA has a fixed per-CSR layout and a
consolidated existence table (Table 13) -- see
`references/spec-mining.md` for the exact headers and extraction recipes.

## Phase 2: classify dispositions

Run `scripts/classify_csr_coverage.py tests/andes_csr/csr_inventory.csv` and
the guard `tests/andes_csr/check_coverage.py`. The guard enforces
inventory == matrix == ABI (`include/hybrid/state_abi.h`), so a CSR added to
the wire format without a disposition (or vice versa) fails loudly. New
transported CSRs are one X-macro line in `state_abi.h`
(`HYBRID_ANDES_CSR_LIST` / `HYBRID_M_EXT_CSR_LIST`); every consumer
(plugin drain, restore, drain re-read, verify) iterates the same list.

## Phase 3: bind capability gates

For each transported CSR, build the three-way translation row (spec
condition <-> RTL `existent_csr` term <-> config macros; see
`references/three-way-audit.md`), then encode it: a gate in the vsim repo's
`src/hybrid/andes_caps.hpp` (address -> gate), the `_NDS_*` binding in
`andes_caps_config.hpp` (absent macro reads as "off" -- never a compile
error), and the same rule in the andesim mirror
`scripts/config_inc_to_andes_caps.py` (the parity guard keeps the two
honest). The gate must encode the RTL's existence term, not a
plausibly-related feature; three real bugs came from getting this wrong
(0x7D1, jvt, 0x7CF/PMNDS). Follow TDD: model the new engine's config shape
as a caps helper in `tests/hybrid/andes_caps.test.cpp` and write the
failing expectation first. Read `references/caps-gating.md` -- it carries
the gate-authoring rules and the write-prerequisite (setup ordering)
requirements.

## Phase 4: reset values and verify exclusions

Two reset-value sources exist and they legitimately differ:
- The SPA reset table (documentation; many fields are IM = implementation
  determined or DC = don't care).
- The EMPIRICAL baseline the simulator drains from the freshly reset hart
  (cached per engine build + ELF). The liveness gate compares against this
  one -- it is self-truthing, so spec IM/DC values need no manual table.

Where QEMU's reset differs from the engine's reset for a CSR the program
never writes (e.g. `msp_bound`, `milmb` enable bit), a strict compare
false-positives: add it to `andes_verify_excluded` in
`driver/state_diff.cpp` with a comment naming the divergence. Do NOT
exclude a CSR to hide a transport bug -- exclusion is only for
engine-implementation artifacts.

## Phase 5: validate (the ladder)

Run bottom-up; each rung catches what the one below cannot. The key
insight: the tolerant abstract path MASKS capability bugs (a faulting read
mirrors as zero, QEMU drains zero too, --verify falsely matches), so caps
truth needs its own empirical rung -- the reset-hart probe (`--probe`, a
checked read of every inventory CSR that reports an unimplemented one as
absent) cross-checked against the caps claim by the manifest completeness
check, which fails NAMING the CSR in either direction. Full commands,
expected outputs, and failure playbook: `references/validation.md`.

## Phase 6: register the engine (per-engine test completeness)

andesim is a commercial product: every supported engine BUILD must ship its
own complete, machine-checked CSR test artifacts -- and a rebuild of the
same core with a different config counts as a NEW registration (the
config.inc hash is the identity, so reuse is impossible by construction).
Four deliverables per engine build: the CSR manifest (every spec CSR:
implemented? transported? why? empirical reset value), a BOTH-direction
completeness check (over-claims fault the sweep; under-claims -- implemented
but not transported and not on a named exclusion -- must fail a script, not
a human's memory), generated per-engine write-survival fixtures, and a
registration guard so an unregistered engine fails loudly. Read
`references/engine-registration.md` for the contract, the file layout, and
the recipes (including what to build the first time the tooling is missing).

## Phase 7: commit and document

TDD and Tidy First apply: caps fixes, sweep/transport changes, and docs are
separate commits, each on a green suite. Update the vsim `ROADMAP.md`
known-limits and `docs/USER_GUIDE.md` (section 4.4 documents what --verify
compares). Update `tests/andes_csr/csr_coverage.csv` through the classifier,
never by hand -- the guard checks policy == matrix.

# The validation ladder

Run bottom-up. Each rung catches what the one below cannot. All vsim
builds/tests run inside the vsim repo's container (built by its
`build_vsim.sh`); the andesim side runs on the host with `config.env`
providing `QEMU_BIN_DIR`/`VSIM_BIN_DIR`.

## 1. Unit suite (seconds)

```sh
podman run --rm -v <vsim-checkout>:/work -w /work localhost/vsim-env:latest \
  bash -c 'cmake --build build -j && ctest --test-dir build -LE hybrid-e2e'
```

Catches: gate-map regressions (andes_caps tests), sweep encoding, X-macro
drift (`test_state_abi` pins the wire format size/offsets -- it changes
whenever a CSR list grows).

## 2. Coverage guard (seconds, andesim repo)

```sh
bash tests/andes_csr/test_csr_coverage_complete.sh
```

Catches: inventory/matrix/ABI drift -- a CSR in the wire format without a
disposition, a disposition for a CSR the ABI dropped, or a hand-edited
matrix that the classifier policy does not reproduce.

## 3. Cold-cache hybrid run = the caps validator (a minute)

```sh
rm -rf ~/.cache/andesim   # force a fresh reset-baseline capture
./andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:<engine> \
  --verify tests/fixtures/rt_c_hello.elf
```

The capture is a FULL drain of the freshly reset hart and its CSR block
rides the batched PB sweep over the COMPLETE caps-supported list -- so a
clean capture empirically proves every claimed CSR is csrr-able on this
RTL. One over-claim aborts the run with the bisected name:

```
[critical] fatal exception: csr_sweep: CSR 0x17 raised cmderr -- the caps
map over-claims a CSR the hart does not implement (fix andes_caps)
```

Fix the named CSR's gate (see caps-gating.md), rebuild, rerun; repeat
until the capture is clean. Expect the `--verify` field count to DROP by
one per de-claimed CSR (e.g. premium went 146 -> 144 when 0x7D1 and 0x017
left the set) -- a drop is correct, those fields were zero-vs-zero
false matches before.

Read the error TEXT as a discriminator: the CSR sweep bisects its batch
faults and rethrows a RENAMED error (`csr_sweep: CSR 0x...`). So a raw
`exec_progbuf: PB execution raised cmderr=3` means the fault is in one of
the NON-CSR Program-Buffer sites instead: the FPR/V data sweeps with
mstatus.FS/VS still Off (flags claim FP/V the engine lacks -- check the
QEMU-side ISA pairing), or a load/store access fault on the scratch page
(memory map does not cover mmap top page). On sim binaries older than the
bisect feature, a raw cmderr=3 can still be the caps map.

## 4. --verify field diffs

`[state-diff] FAIL` lines name mismatching fields. Triage order:
- Field never restored/re-read? Missing from an X-macro consumer (should
  be impossible if the lists are used) or caps-gated off on one side.
- Value differs only at reset (program never writes it)? Check
  QEMU-vs-engine reset divergence -> `andes_verify_excluded` in
  `driver/state_diff.cpp`, WITH a comment naming the divergence
  (precedents: msp_bound/msp_base all-ones-vs-zero, milmb/mdlmb enable
  bit, mip timer bit). Exclusion is for engine artifacts only -- never to
  hide a transport bug.
- Hardware counters that tick during the ROI (mhpmcounter*) are
  transported but verify-excluded by design, like mcycle.

## 5. Full e2e matrix (minutes)

```sh
QEMU_BIN_DIR=... VSIM_BIN_DIR=... VSIM_QEMU=... VSIM_QEMU32=... \
VSIM_PLUGIN=<andesim>/qemu_plugin/libhybrid_handoff.so \
JOBS=8 bash scripts/run_e2e.sh
```

Env vars must be on the command line (they do not persist between shells;
`source setup.sh` piped into anything loses its exports). JOBS=8 caps the
Verilator process count on big machines. Expect all tests green across
marker + pc + neg; the S/U fixtures (rt_priv_*) run on the S/U-capable
engine and take ~80 s each.

## Cost model (why the sweep matters)

Every Debug-Module operation (abstract command or PB exec) costs ~200-900
SIMULATED cycles at ~10 kHz wall speed, so full-drain wall-clock is
dominated by DM op COUNT, not bytes:
- GPR/FPR: PB block sweeps, ~6 round-trips each instead of 31/32 ops.
- Andes+M-ext CSRs: batched csrr+sd sweep, 3 CSRs per PB exec (progbufsize
  8 -> (8-1)/2), values ride the shared scratch page.
- Minimal drain (no --verify) skips all of it: only mcycle/minstret.
- The liveness gate (reset baseline) elides restores whose drained value
  equals the engine's reset value; the baseline is captured once per
  (engine build, ELF) and cached under `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/andesim/`
  (`--no-reset-baseline` to disable; the cache key includes the sim
  binary's mtime+size, so rebuilds self-invalidate).

## Sweep/lift invariants (when touching the transport itself)

- The drain sweep runs only on FULL drains; the simulator lifts the swept
  scratch bytes (`read_csr_from_scratch`) under EXACTLY the same condition
  the drain used to choose sweep-vs-abstract (`csr_scratch_fits`, flags,
  and not-minimal) -- a lift without a sweep reads garbage; a sweep
  without a lift silently loses in-ROI CSR writes.
- Scratch page layout (top page of RAM): V data grows up from the base;
  GPR block at the top, FPR below it, CSR block below that. Every user is
  fits-gated on the live vlenb so a full V page falls back to abstract
  ops on both sides symmetrically.

## Cost model (why drain cost never taints the figure)

Every Debug-Module operation (abstract command or PB exec) costs ~200-900
SIMULATED cycles at ~10 kHz wall speed, so full-drain wall-clock is
dominated by DM op COUNT, not bytes:
- GPRs, FPRs, and every transported CSR: one abstract command each, both
  directions (a full drain is ~190 abstract ops). Only the V regfile rides
  the Program Buffer + shared scratch page.
- The cycle figure is unaffected either way: mcycle/minstret are read
  BEFORE the CSR/L2C/V drain work, and the drain runs after the exit
  trigger, outside the measured window.
- Minimal drain (no --verify) skips all of it: only mcycle/minstret.
- The liveness gate (reset baseline) elides restores whose drained value
  equals the engine's reset value; the baseline is captured once per
  (engine build, ELF) and cached under `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/andesim/`
  (`--no-reset-baseline` to disable; the cache key includes the sim
  binary's mtime+size, so rebuilds self-invalidate).

## Scratch-page invariants (when touching the transport itself)

- The scratch page (top page of the mapped RAM span) carries ONLY the V
  data regfile: staged by `stage_v_to_scratch` before resume, dumped by
  the drain's vse8 sweep, lifted by `read_v_from_scratch`. GPRs, FPRs, and
  CSRs never touch it -- they move over DMI directly.
- The V dump sweep runs LAST in the drain (after every architectural
  read), so its clobbers (vtype/vl/vstart, x5/x6/x7) and counter ticks
  cannot corrupt already-captured state.

# The validation ladder

Run bottom-up. Each rung catches what the one below cannot. All vsim
builds/tests run inside the vsim repo's container (built by its
`build_vsim.sh`); the andesim side runs on the host with `config.env`
providing `QEMU_BIN_DIR`/`VSIM_BIN_DIR`.

## 1. Unit suite (seconds)

```sh
podman run --rm -v <vsim-checkout>:/work -w /work localhost/vsim-env:latest \
  bash -c 'cmake --build build -j && ctest --test-dir build -LE hybrid-e2e'
```

Catches: gate-map regressions (andes_caps tests), transport orchestration
(abstract-only contract tests, V sweep / L2C encodings), X-macro drift
(`test_state_abi` pins the wire format size/offsets -- it changes whenever
a CSR list grows).

## 2. Coverage guard (seconds, andesim repo)

```sh
bash tests/andes_csr/test_csr_coverage_complete.sh
```

Catches: inventory/matrix/ABI drift -- a CSR in the wire format without a
disposition, a disposition for a CSR the ABI dropped, or a hand-edited
matrix that the classifier policy does not reproduce.

## 3. Probe + manifest completeness check = the caps validator (a minute)

Transport never faults on a caps over-claim -- every GPR/FPR/CSR moves via
one TOLERANT Abstract Command (restore clears the cmderr and moves on;
drain's checked read mirrors an absent CSR as zero) -- so caps truth needs
its own empirical rung:

```sh
bash tests/engines/probe_engine.sh <engine>   # -> sim_<engine> --probe
python3 tests/engines/gen_manifest.py tests/engines/<engine>-<confighash8>/
```

The probe checked-reads EVERY inventory CSR on the halted, freshly reset
hart; an unimplemented CSR surfaces as absent (nullopt), an implemented one
yields its empirical reset value. The manifest generator cross-checks the
probe against the caps claim (`--describe andes_csrs`) and the coverage
matrix, and fails NAMING the CSR in either direction:
- Over-claim (caps yes, probe absent): fix the named CSR's gate (see
  caps-gating.md), rebuild, re-probe. Expect the `--verify` field count to
  DROP by one per de-claimed CSR (e.g. premium went 146 -> 144 when 0x7D1
  and 0x017 left the set) -- a drop is correct, those fields were
  zero-vs-zero false matches before.
- Under-claim (probe present, not transported, no named EXCL_*): add the
  gate/disposition -- this is the silent state-loss case.

cmderr discriminator for a hybrid run that DOES abort with
`exec_progbuf: PB execution raised cmderr=3`: the fault is in one of the
few remaining Program-Buffer sites -- the V data sweep with mstatus.VS
still Off (flags claim V the engine lacks -- check the QEMU-side ISA
pairing), the Tier-B vsetvl, a load/store access fault on the scratch page
(memory map does not cover the mmap top page), or an L2C MMIO access on an
engine without an L2C. It is never a CSR caps problem -- CSR faults are
tolerated and cleared (ResumeDriver's cmderr diagnostics count them).

## 4. Cold-cache --verify run (round-trip proof, a minute)

```sh
rm -rf ~/.cache/andesim   # force a fresh reset-baseline capture
./andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:<engine> \

```

# Capability gating: mapping IM Requirements to engine gates

Three files, three roles (all in the vsim repo):

| File | Role |
|------|------|
| `src/hybrid/andes_caps.hpp` | CSR address -> `AndesGate` (spec knowledge, engine-free, unit-testable) |
| `src/hybrid/andes_caps_config.hpp` | `AndesGate` -> `_NDS_*` config macro (the one binding site) |
| `build/V<engine>/obj_sc/config.inc` | what THIS engine actually has (ground truth) |

A CSR with no case in `andes_gate_for` defaults to ALWAYS = transported
unconditionally. Every CSR added to the ABI lists therefore needs a
deliberate decision: ALWAYS only for base machine CSRs every Andes core
has (mxstatus, mclk_ctl, mdcause).

## The rules (each one paid for by a real bug)

# The three-way audit: spec x config x RTL

Validating a vsim engine's CSR transport means proving THREE sources agree,
per CSR. Each answers a different question, and any two can agree while
being wrong -- only the triangle closes the audit:

| Source | Where | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| 1. SPEC (SPA PDF) | per-CSR `IM Requirement:` + Table 13 | when does the CSR exist, in ARCHITECTURE terms (`mmsc_cfg.PMNDS & misa[20]`) |
| 2. CONFIG (vsim config) | `build/V<engine>/obj_sc/config.inc` | which knobs THIS build turned on (`NDS_*` macros) |
| 3. CPU CORE (RTL) | the decoder's `existent_csr` equation | the EXACT mapping: spec condition as a function of config params |

The RTL is the Rosetta stone. The spec speaks architecture
(`mmsc_cfg.PMNDS`), the config speaks knobs (`NDS_PERFORMANCE_MONITOR_INT`),
and nothing in either document says how one maps to the other. The decoder
equation does -- it is the hardware's own translation, one term per CSR.

## Step 1: find the decoder equation

```sh
grep -rln existent_csr $VSIM_BIN_DIR/../V<engine>/  # kv_core family:
# andes_ip/kv_core/ucore/hdl/kv_csr_dec.v
grep -o "(csr_addr == 12'h7cf)[^|]*" .../kv_csr_dec.v
```

Decoder generations differ: some write hex literals (`12'h7cf`), others
symbolic names (`CSR12_MCOUNTERINTEN` -- premium's does). An empty grep
means your PATTERN missed, not that the CSR is absent: grep the NAME too
before concluding anything (a class-A trap; see the disagreement table).

Real terms from ax46mpv_advanced (line-wrapped):

```
(csr_addr == 12'h7cf) & (PERFORMANCE_MONITOR_INT == 1) & (SSCOFPMF_SUPPORT == 0)
(csr_addr == 12'h7d1) & (PERFORMANCE_MONITOR_INT == 1) & (SSCOFPMF_SUPPORT == 0) & multi_level_mode
(csr_addr == 12'h017) & (ZCE_SUPPORT_INT == 1)
(csr_addr == 12'h7c5) & (POWERBRAKE_SUPPORT_INT == 1)
```

## Step 2: build the translation table

For every transported CSR, one row connecting all three languages:

| CSR | Spec condition | RTL term | config.inc knobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| mcounterinten 0x7CF | `mmsc_cfg.PMNDS==1` | `PERF_MONITOR & !SSCOFPMF` | `NDS_PERFORMANCE_MONITOR_INT`, `NDS_SSCOFPMF_SUPPORT` |
| mcountermask_m 0x7D1 | `PMNDS & misa[20]` | `PERF & !SSCOFPMF & multi_level_mode` | + `NDS_NUM_PRIVILEGE_LEVELS >= 2` |
| jvt 0x017 | Zcmt implemented | `ZCE_SUPPORT_INT == 1` | `NDS_ZCE_SUPPORT_INT` |

The translation is where every real bug so far has lived:
- spec `PMNDS` is NOT the config's `PERFORMANCE_MONITOR` knob -- it is
  `PERF && !SSCOFPMF` (the standard Sscofpmf scheme REPLACES the Andes
  counters). Gating 0x7CF on the perf knob alone over-claimed it on the
  Sscofpmf-bearing advanced engine and faulted the sweep.

# The three-way audit: spec x config x RTL

Validating a vsim engine's CSR transport means proving THREE sources agree,
per CSR. Each answers a different question, and any two can agree while
being wrong -- only the triangle closes the audit:

| Source | Where | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| 1. SPEC (SPA PDF) | per-CSR `IM Requirement:` + Table 13 | when does the CSR exist, in ARCHITECTURE terms (`mmsc_cfg.PMNDS & misa[20]`) |
| 2. CONFIG (vsim config) | `build/V<engine>/obj_sc/config.inc` | which knobs THIS build turned on (`NDS_*` macros) |
| 3. CPU CORE (RTL) | the decoder's `existent_csr` equation | the EXACT mapping: spec condition as a function of config params |

The RTL is the Rosetta stone. The spec speaks architecture
(`mmsc_cfg.PMNDS`), the config speaks knobs (`NDS_PERFORMANCE_MONITOR_INT`),
and nothing in either document says how one maps to the other. The decoder
equation does -- it is the hardware's own translation, one term per CSR.

## Step 1: find the decoder equation

```sh
grep -rln existent_csr $VSIM_BIN_DIR/../V<engine>/  # kv_core family:
# andes_ip/kv_core/ucore/hdl/kv_csr_dec.v
grep -o "(csr_addr == 12'h7cf)[^|]*" .../kv_csr_dec.v
```

Decoder generations differ: some write hex literals (`12'h7cf`), others
symbolic names (`CSR12_MCOUNTERINTEN` -- premium's does). An empty grep
means your PATTERN missed, not that the CSR is absent: grep the NAME too
before concluding anything (a class-A trap; see the disagreement table).

Real terms from ax46mpv_advanced (line-wrapped):

```
(csr_addr == 12'h7cf) & (PERFORMANCE_MONITOR_INT == 1) & (SSCOFPMF_SUPPORT == 0)
(csr_addr == 12'h7d1) & (PERFORMANCE_MONITOR_INT == 1) & (SSCOFPMF_SUPPORT == 0) & multi_level_mode
(csr_addr == 12'h017) & (ZCE_SUPPORT_INT == 1)
(csr_addr == 12'h7c5) & (POWERBRAKE_SUPPORT_INT == 1)
```

## Step 2: build the translation table

For every transported CSR, one row connecting all three languages:

| CSR | Spec condition | RTL term | config.inc knobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| mcounterinten 0x7CF | `mmsc_cfg.PMNDS==1` | `PERF_MONITOR & !SSCOFPMF` | `NDS_PERFORMANCE_MONITOR_INT`, `NDS_SSCOFPMF_SUPPORT` |
| mcountermask_m 0x7D1 | `PMNDS & misa[20]` | `PERF & !SSCOFPMF & multi_level_mode` | + `NDS_NUM_PRIVILEGE_LEVELS >= 2` |
| jvt 0x017 | Zcmt implemented | `ZCE_SUPPORT_INT == 1` | `NDS_ZCE_SUPPORT_INT` |

The translation is where every real bug so far has lived:
- spec `PMNDS` is NOT the config's `PERFORMANCE_MONITOR` knob -- it is
  `PERF && !SSCOFPMF` (the standard Sscofpmf scheme REPLACES the Andes
  counters). Gating 0x7CF on the perf knob alone over-claimed it on the
  Sscofpmf-bearing advanced engine.
- spec "User mode implemented" (`misa[20]`) is `NDS_NUM_PRIVILEGE_LEVELS >= 2`.
- spec "Zcmt" is the `ZCE_SUPPORT` knob, NOT the CoDense knob.

## Step 3: encode the row as code (TDD)

Each row lands in FOUR places that must never drift:
1. vsim gate map: `src/hybrid/andes_caps.hpp` (`andes_gate_for`)
2. vsim knob binding: `src/hybrid/andes_caps_config.hpp`
3. andesim offline mirror: `scripts/config_inc_to_andes_caps.py`
4. the caps unit test modeling THIS engine's config shape
   (`tests/hybrid/andes_caps.test.cpp` -- see the `premium()`/`advanced()`
   helpers; write the failing expectation FIRST)

Drift between 1+2 and 3 is caught by the parity guard
(`tests/andes_sim/test_andes_sim_caps_parity.sh`, all built engines).
Drift between the code and the RTL is caught only by Step 4.

## Step 4: confirm against the live engine

Paper agreement is not validation -- the parity guard passed while BOTH
sides over-claimed 0x7CF together. The empirical check is the reset-hart
probe, which checked-reads every inventory CSR on the RTL (an
unimplemented CSR reports as absent -- transport itself never faults on
one, so a run "not crashing" proves nothing about caps):

```sh
bash tests/engines/probe_engine.sh <engine>       # sim_<engine> --probe
python3 tests/engines/gen_manifest.py tests/engines/<engine>-<confighash8>/
rm -rf ~/.cache/andesim                           # then prove the round-trip
./andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:<engine> \
  --verify tests/fixtures/rt_c_hello.elf
```

- Over-claim -> the manifest completeness check fails NAMING the CSR
  (caps claims it, the probe reports it absent) -> back to Step 1 for that
  CSR.
- Under-claim -> the same check, other direction (see
  engine-registration.md deliverable 2): every probe-present,
  spec-transportable CSR must be claimed or on a named exclusion.
- Clean check + `[verify] PASS` -> the engine's claimed set is proven
  implemented and round-trips. Expect the compared-field count to differ
  per engine -- the caps decide the set; the current count is in each
  engine's `registration_report.md`.

## Step 5: write the engine's test cases

A validated engine gets registered with its own permanent tests
(engine-registration.md has the full contract):
- the caps unit-test helper modeling its config shape (Step 3.4) -- pins the
  translation table in code;
- the parity guard picks the engine up automatically (it loops over built
  `sim_*` binaries);
- the registration manifest (every spec CSR: exists/transported/why +
  empirical reset value) + generated write-survival fixtures;
- a probe + cold-cache `--verify` run in both trigger modes in the suite,
  so the empirical validation re-runs on every engine rebuild (the baseline
  cache key includes the binary identity -- a rebuild self-invalidates and
  re-proves).

## When the triangle does not close: classify, do not assume

A mismatch has FOUR possible root causes, and the audit must say which --
"fix the caps map" is the shipping action, not the diagnosis:

| Class | Signature | Action |
|---|---|---|
| A. Interpretation error (yours) | two readings of the SAME source disagree: per-CSR section vs Table 13, or your RTL-equation reading vs the empirical probe | re-extract with the second method; if still conflicting, mark UNRESOLVED in the report -- never guess. PDF table flattening (Table 13's stacked rows) and truncated greps of the long `existent_csr` line are the usual culprits |
| B. QEMU-model artifact | RTL + spec agree; QEMU differs (it models no local memory, different reset defaults) | verify-exclude with a named reason (precedents: milmb/mdlmb EN bit, msp_bound reset). Not an RTL bug -- do not escalate to the RTL team |
| C. Suspected RTL bug / undocumented deviation | RTL and the empirical probe agree with EACH OTHER but contradict the spec's clear condition, while QEMU follows the spec | transport follows the ENGINE (ship), and the discrepancy is ESCALATED to the RTL owners with the quoted equation + spec text. Never silently absorb it |
| D. Suspected spec error / ambiguity | independent implementations (RTL AND QEMU) agree against the spec text, or the spec self-contradicts | record the chosen reading + escalate to the spec owners |

Triangulation levers, cheapest first: (1) re-read the same source a second
way (section vs Table 13; grep vs the probe); (2) QEMU as an independent
implementation of the same spec; (3) sibling engines (does premium's RTL
carry the same term?); (4) the empirical sweep/probe -- execution evidence
outranks any reading.

Evidence standard for the report: verbatim quotes with file:line / PDF
page for every claim in a discrepancy row. A paraphrase cannot be
re-audited, and class A errors hide in paraphrases.

## Worked example: the 0x7CF find, end to end

1. Symptom: first-ever hybrid run on ax46mpv_advanced died:
   `csr_sweep: CSR 0x7cf raised cmderr -- the caps map over-claims...`
2. Config check: `NDS_PERFORMANCE_MONITOR_INT 1` on BOTH engines -- the knob
   cannot explain premium-works/advanced-faults. So the gate's model of the
   world is wrong, not the config.
3. RTL: grep the advanced decoder -> `0x7cf ... & (SSCOFPMF_SUPPORT == 0)`;
   advanced config.inc: `NDS_SSCOFPMF_SUPPORT 1` (premium: 0). Root cause.
4. Spec cross-check: SPA Table 13 gates the block on `mmsc_cfg.PMNDS`; the
   RTL term IS the PMNDS definition in config language.
5. Fix: PMNDS/PMNDS_UMODE/PMNDS_SMODE gates (vsim + Python mirror), RED
   test first with an `advanced()` config-shape helper.
6. Validate: parity on both engines, cold-cache `--verify` PASS on both
   (advanced: first successful hybrid run, 145 fields), full e2e.

# Engine registration: per-engine, per-config test completeness

The authoritative contract lives IN THE REPO at `tests/engines/README.md`
(registration inputs/artifacts/checks, the report format including the
mandatory Discrepancies section, and the deregistration checklist for
removing an engine + its report + its test cases). This reference explains
the mechanics behind it. If the two ever disagree, the repo contract wins
-- update this file.

andesim ships commercially. "The transport machinery is tested" is not the
same as "THIS engine build's CSR set is tested" -- every engine can differ
in its CSR set, and the same core built with a different config differs
again. Registration turns "nothing missed" from a convention into a set of
checks that fail.

## Identity: an engine build = (core, config)

The registration key is the engine name plus a short hash of the BUILD
`config.inc` (`build/V<engine>/obj_sc/config.inc` -- the file Phase 0
already reads). Layout in the andesim repo:

```
tests/engines/<engine>-<confighash8>/
├── engine.env               # engine name, QEMU -cpu pairing, march, vlen, priv levels
├── rtl_params.json          # resolved RTL params: data for the shared generator's
│                            #   EXCL_SIDEFX-only RTL fallback (provenance in "notes")
├── csr_manifest.csv         # deliverable 1 (tests/engines/gen_manifest.py <regdir>;
│                            #   the shared generator auto-runs the probe)
├── csr_restore_table.md     # human-readable restore view of the manifest
│                            #   (generated by render_restore_table.py; drift-guarded)
├── registration_report.md   # the CSR report (see the repo contract)
└── fixtures/                # deliverable 3 (generated)
```

A rebuilt config produces a different hash -> a different directory -> the
guard (deliverable 4) refuses to run the engine against the old artifacts.
Nothing about "same core, new config" can be silently reused.

## Deliverable 1: the CSR manifest

0x7D1,mcountermask_m,MRW,PMNDS&misa[20],no,no,UMODE(off),-
0x7CF,mcounterinten,MRW,PMNDS,yes,yes,PERF_MONITOR,0x0
...
```

`python3 tests/engines/gen_manifest.py <regdir>` -- which reads the regdir's
`engine.env` (identity) and `rtl_params.json` (resolved RTL params for the
SIDEFX-only fallback below). There is no per-engine generator code.

  is expected and fine), then committed.

  the cold-cache capture's CSR sweep faults and names the CSR. Keep a

freshly reset hart (the DM mirrors an unimplemented CSR as a cmderr, which

- WARL-constrained: write within a reviewed mask;
- dangerous control CSRs: skip-list with a comment saying why -- the
  round-trip of these is still covered by --verify on real workload values.

must have a `tests/engines/<engine>-<confighash8>/` whose hash matches the
CURRENT binary's config.inc, with a manifest and generated fixtures
present. Unregistered or stale-hash engines fail with "run the bring-up
registration". Wire it next to the existing coverage guard so CI runs both.

The full 47-fixture suite stays on the default engines (wall-time). Every
REGISTERED engine runs its own core set on every suite run: the probe
check, its generated CSR fixtures, a cold-cache hybrid run (the sweep
validator), and one --verify run. `run_e2e.sh` takes the engine axis from
the registration dirs, so adding a registration automatically adds its
tests -- no runner edit, nothing to forget.

---
name: csr-transport-bringup
description: >
  Bring up or audit the hybrid CSR transport for an Andes RISC-V core, given
  the AndeStar V5 SPA PDF spec and a built vsim engine. Covers the whole
  pipeline: mine the spec (CSR inventory, IM Requirement / existence
  conditions, access modes, reset values), classify transport dispositions,
  bind capability gates to the engine's config.inc, and validate with the
  reset-hart CSR probe (--probe), the manifest completeness check, --verify,
  and the e2e suite. Use this skill whenever the user mentions a new core, a
  new vsim engine, CSR transport / transportation, CSR capability or caps
  gating, IM Requirement, reset value table, which mode a CSR is supported
  in, probe-vs-caps mismatches, exec_progbuf cmderr faults, or --verify
  field mismatches on Andes/M-ext CSRs -- even if they do not say "bring-up"
  explicitly. Also use it for engine registration work: per-engine test
  files, CSR manifests, completeness ("nothing missed") checks, or adding a
  new config of an existing core.
---

# CSR transport bring-up for a new Andes core

Inputs you need from the user (ask if missing):
- The AndeStar V5 SPA PDF for the core family (the repo carries
  `AndeStar_V5_SPA_UM164_V1.7.pdf` for the current cores).
- The engine name (e.g. `ax45mpv_premium`) and a built vsim checkout
  (`VSIM_BIN_DIR` in `config.env` points at its `build/`).
- Optionally the matching QEMU `-cpu` name for the oracle leg.

The goal: every CSR the core implements and the ROI can touch is restored at
resume, re-read at drain, and `--verify`-compared -- and every CSR the core
does NOT implement is gated off. Getting the gate wrong is SILENT at run
time: transport is one tolerant Abstract Command per CSR in both directions
(the Program Buffer carries only the V data sweep, the Tier-B vsetvl, and
L2C MMIO), so an over-claimed CSR just mirrors as zero. Caps truth is proven
by the reset-hart probe + the manifest completeness check, never by a run
"not crashing".

Work in this order. Each phase has a reference file with the details --
read it when you reach the phase, not before.

## Phase 0: establish ground truth (three sources)

Validation means connecting THREE sources per CSR -- the spec, the build
config, and the CPU core RTL -- and they speak different languages:
- CONFIG: `$VSIM_BIN_DIR/V<engine>/obj_sc/config.inc` (the BUILD copy -- the
  `external/` source tree can differ) + `sim_<engine> --describe`.
- RTL: the CSR decoder's `existent_csr` equation (kv_core family:
  `andes_ip/kv_core/ucore/hdl/kv_csr_dec.v`). This is the Rosetta stone: it
  states each spec existence condition as a function of config params --
  the mapping neither document contains.
- SPEC: Phase 1 below.
Read `references/three-way-audit.md` -- the tutorial for connecting the
three and turning the result into the engine's test cases. Do not trust
QEMU: its gdbstub exposes CSRs the vsim RTL does not implement, and
restoring or sweeping one of those stalls or faults the Debug Module.

## Phase 1: mine the spec

Run `scripts/extract_csr_inventory.py <spec.pdf>` to refresh
`tests/andes_csr/csr_inventory.csv` (needs PyMuPDF; use a venv). Then pull,
for each CSR the core claims: the IM Requirement (existence condition), the
Access Mode, and the reset value. The SPA has a fixed per-CSR layout and a
consolidated existence table (Table 13) -- see
`references/spec-mining.md` for the exact headers and extraction recipes.

## Phase 2: classify dispositions

這是一個你之前寫到一半的 v6 write-mask 功能:**「guest 寫過但引擎不支援的 CSR」警告**。內容:

- **新函式 `unsupported_written_csrs(state, andes_supported)`**(`state_diff.cpp/.hpp`,+59 行):拿 v6 write-mask(guest 真的執行過 csrw 的紀錄)對照引擎的 supported 清單(`--describe andes_csrs`),找出「程式有寫、但 cycle engine 沒實作」的 CSR。
- **意義**(header 註解寫得很清楚):這是真實的不相容訊號 -- 在那顆引擎的實體晶片上,這個 csrw 會在 boot 時 trap,程式根本跑不到 ROI;但 hybrid restore 只是靜默跳過。driver 應該用這些名字發警告。
- 細節:`ucode` 不報(plugin 無條件設它的 bit,不是真寫入紀錄);PMA 以 `pmacfg`/`pmaaddr` 群組名回報;pre-v6 檔案或沒有引擎資訊時回傳空。
- **測試已寫好**(`state_diff_test.cpp`,+42 行):不支援的寫入會列名、全支援時為空、無引擎資訊為空、pre-v6 為空。

**未完成的部分**:grep 不到任何呼叫者 -- driver 端(應該是 `cmd_run.cpp`)還沒接上這個函式發警告,所以功能只有 library + tests,還沒生效。這大概就是它掛在 working tree 沒 commit 的原因。

順帶一提:這個功能跟這次的 sweep 移除完全相容(它讀 write-mask 和 supported 清單,不碰 transport 機制)。要我把 driver 端的警告接完再一起 commit,還是先照現狀 commit?

8	//            mepc/mcause (round-trip), mscratch (L23) + mtval/mie (L24) --

11	//            and the vreg bytes under FLAG_V.
12	//   skipped: mstatus, mtvec, medeleg, mideleg, mip, satp, pmpcfg[], pmpaddr[].
13	//            mtvec/medeleg/mideleg/satp/PMP are passthrough on the vsim side
14	//            (copied from QEMU1's ENTRY snapshot, never re-read). mip IS
15	//            re-read but excluded here -- its pending bits are hardware-driven
16	//            and diverge between the engines' clocks. mstatus is excluded for
17	//            its dirty/impl-defined bits.
18	//   masked:  mcycle, minstret -- the engines count cycles/insns differently

34	  unsigned long long ref = 0;
35	  unsigned long long got = 0;
36	};

The handoff also carries the **v6 write-mask**: the plugin tracks which config
CSRs (the Andes block, PMA, the M-ext block, `mcache_ctl`/`mmisc_ctl`) your
program actually WROTE, and the cycle engine restores -- and `--verify`
compares -- only those. A CSR the program never touched keeps the engine's own
reset value instead of inheriting QEMU's reset default, so reset-value
differences between QEMU and any engine cannot skew the run. The tracking is
translation-time work in the plugin (only CSR-write instructions get a
callback), so the fast leg's speed is unaffected.

The write-mask also powers an **incompatibility warning** on every hybrid run
(not just `--verify`): if your program wrote a config CSR the chosen cycle
engine does not implement, the driver prints

```
[andesim] warning: the program wrote CSRs engine vsim:<engine> does not
implement: <names> (on this engine's silicon these writes would trap; the
hybrid restore skipped them)
```

to stderr. On that engine's real silicon the `csrw` would trap before the ROI,
so the cycle figure may not represent this program on this engine -- pick an
engine that implements those CSRs, or drop the writes. A clean run prints
nothing.
